The past week has been a nonstop parade of important network outages, from a big Microsoft fiasco to the FAA grounding planes and more, including network issues at the NSA and JPMorgan Chase & Co. Now, it looks like it’s Apple’s turn.

For the last couple of hours, several of Apple’s network services have been experiencing problems. The System Status page has shown various services in various states of operation, from iCloud Mail to Apple Music and News, though most of them have returned to “green” status. Several internal Apple networking services for employees are said to be affected as well.

At the time of this writing, there are scattered issues with some of the School Management services and AppleCare’s on-device signup, volume purchases, and the App Store. It is not clear how widespread these issues are, however, and two of our editors in the U.S. were able to use the App Store just fine, for example.

In a statement to Bloomberg, Apple said, “Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning. We’re working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible.” Apple also said the problems do not stem from a cyberattack, echoing the sentiment from Microsoft and others. Apparently it’s just been a really bad week.

In October, Apple announced that it was going to change how it implements Full Disk Access control in macOS. Users were going to have to perform “very explicit user action” to grant FDA to an app, which is a change from before, when apps could prompt users to flip switches on in System Settings to allow FDA.

The change is coming to macOS 27.3, and it was recently unveiled in the macOS 27.3 beta 2 that was released on Monday. Apple released a note to developers notifying them about the change, stating that the changes “empower [users] to make informed decisions about their own data and privacy.”

The new FDA UI was posted online by madeby_ldt, and it’s much more detailed and explicit. When an app asks for FDA, users will now be able to see what data the app wants to collect and grant permission to certain types of access. For example, the ChatGPT app wants access to be able to “Read, Change, Delete, and Export All Your Data,” “View Hidden and Recently Deleted Photos,” and “View History and Browse as You.” You’ll be able to allow or deny access to each of those requests.

The example provided uses ChatGPT, which is no coincidence. Chatbots and other AI apps want as much access to your data as they can get—it’s how they function and are able to tailor responses to your specific needs. AI apps aren’t the only ones that want FDA, but they grow more popular every day, and a lot of users are naive about how they work. Apple’s changes to FDA are one way to bring awareness of AI demands to the user.

Apple is expected to release macOS 27.3 in early December. Keep track of the latest with macOS 27 in our superguide.

Test X-VPN's new speed boost for yourself for free

Combined download and upload improvements of 200%

Learn more

A VPN encrypts your traffic and sends it through another server, which usually costs some speed. The speed upgrade built around X-VPN‘s new Talaria protocol reduces that speed cost, and its published tests include impressive Mac results. (A protocol is the set of rules a VPN uses to connect and encrypt your data.)

What is Talaria?

Talaria is X-VPN’s in-house, open-source VPN protocol. It is available on macOS, Windows, iOS and Android, for Free and Premium users, and you need the latest version of the app.

X-VPN

How much faster is it on a Mac?

X-VPN’s macOS tests used an Apple M4 Mac mini on a wired connection.

On a 10Gbps connection, median download speeds (the middle result across repeated tests) rose from between 543 and 753 Mbps with X-VPN’s previous Everest-UDP protocol to between 3,661 and 5,437 Mbps with Talaria, depending on the server.

On a 1Gbps connection, Talaria kept 98.2% to 98.7% of the download speed measured without a VPN, a loss of 1.3% to 1.8%.

X-VPN’s headline figure is an overall improvement of over 200%. That averages combined download and upload improvements across its wider 10Gbps test set, covering Windows, macOS, iOS and Android, so it isn’t a Mac-only number.

X-VPN

Where will Mac users notice it?

Downloading large files. X-VPN says Talaria reduces download times for things like 4K films and system updates. If you keep the VPN on during a big download, that is where waiting time should drop. X-VPN gives no figure for the reduction.

Using a fast home connection. On a 1Gbps plan, the 98% result means most of the speed you pay for stays intact with the VPN on.

Apple HomeView is Apple’s first dedicated smart-home display, combining a 7-inch touchscreen, powerful speakers, a camera, and Siri AI in a device designed to sit at the center of the connected home. Announced on October 13, 2026 and on sale from November 13, it brings together smart-home controls, entertainment, video calling, calendars, reminders, and other everyday information.

Powered by Apple’s A18 chip and Apple Intelligence, HomeView offers a much more capable version of Siri that can answer questions conversationally, help with everyday tasks, and access personal information from a compatible iPhone or iPad. It can also recognize up to six members of a household, providing a personalized experience while keeping individual information private. However, some early owners have reported problems with Siri and other software features, as we explain below.

HomeView is designed to work alongside Apple’s existing HomePod speakers, Apple TV, iPhone, and iPad. It integrates with the Apple Home app, supporting compatible HomeKit and Matter accessories, including lights, locks, thermostats, and security cameras. It can also serve as a central smart-home hub, making it easier to manage devices and automations throughout the house.

Unlike a HomePod with a screen added, HomeView is designed around visual interaction as well as voice control. Its touchscreen, customizable widgets, FaceTime camera, personalized Home Screens, and dedicated smart-home dashboards make it more like a shared household computer than a conventional smart speaker. It comes in tabletop and wall-mounted versions, with prices starting at $299/£299.

What can Apple HomeView do?

HomeView introduces a range of capabilities that aren’t available on Apple’s traditional HomePod speakers. While HomePod focuses primarily on music, Siri, and voice-controlled smart-home functions, HomeView adds a touchscreen, camera, personalized interface, and much deeper integration with Apple apps and services.

HomeView also supports Handoff from iPhone, Live Activities, Find My, and multiroom audio with compatible AirPlay speakers.

How does HomeView compare with HomePod and iPad?

The biggest difference between HomeView and HomePod is the display. While a HomePod can control smart-home devices and play music using Siri, HomeView provides an interactive dashboard and visual feedback, making it more useful for managing a busy household.

HomeView also offers capabilities that make it a potential alternative to an iPad in certain situations. It can display recipes, calendars, photos, and video calls without needing someone to pick it up or unlock it. Its ability to recognize different household members and switch automatically between personalized experiences is particularly useful in a shared space.

However, HomeView isn’t intended to replace an iPad. The iPad remains the better choice for portable computing, productivity, games, and the broad selection of apps available from the App Store. HomeView is designed to stay in one place and provide convenient access to household information, entertainment, and smart-home controls.

Apple HomeView release date: When did it launch?

  • Announced: October 13, 2026
  • Pre-orders: October 13, 2026
  • In Store: November 13, 2026

Apple announced HomeView on Tuesday, October 13, 2026, as part of its “Welcome home” launch. Pre-orders opened the same day, with both the tabletop and wall-mounted models on sale from Friday, November 13.

HomeView is initially available in the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, India, New Zealand, Singapore, and South Africa. Singapore pre-orders opened on October 15, while customers in South Africa can order through authorized resellers.

The device won’t initially be sold in the European Union because Siri AI isn’t currently available in iOS in the EU. Apple says it is working toward resolving the situation, but hasn’t announced a European release date.

HomeView can be ordered from the Apple website, Apple Store app, and selected retailers. It will also be displayed in Apple Stores. Does Apple HomeView have a camera?

The built-in camera cannot double as a security camera or provide an Echo Show-style video Drop In feature. HomeView can display feeds from compatible external security cameras, but that is a separate capability.

Each has two full-range drivers in the display, while the tabletop model adds a down-firing woofer and two force-canceling passive radiators in its base. The wall-mounted version omits this speaker base, with Apple tuning its computational audio specifically for placement against a wall.

What processor does Apple HomeView use?

HomeView is powered by Apple’s A18 chip, the same generation of processor introduced with the iPhone 16 in 2024. This is considerably more powerful than the Apple Watch-derived processors used in older HomePod models and gives HomeView the processing capabilities needed for Apple Intelligence and Siri AI.

The A18 is manufactured using a second-generation 3-nanometer process. In its original iPhone implementation, it features a six-core CPU, five-core GPU, and 16-core Neural Engine. Apple hasn’t confirmed whether the HomeView uses exactly the same CPU and GPU configuration, or whether the chip has been adapted for the new device.

The Neural Engine is particularly important because HomeView uses AI to support conversational Siri interactions, recognize household members, process camera and microphone information, and provide personalized responses. Apple hasn’t revealed any performance comparisons between HomeView and previous HomePod processors, or disclosed any HomeView-specific improvements to chip packaging or manufacturing. Apple HomeView connectivity and compatibility

HomeView supports Wi-Fi 6E, Bluetooth 6.0, and Thread networking, giving it the wireless connectivity needed to communicate with Apple devices and compatible smart-home accessories.

HomeView integrates directly with Apple’s Home app and can control compatible smart lights, door locks, thermostats, blinds, and security cameras. It also supports Matter accessories, expanding compatibility beyond devices specifically designed for HomeKit.

Importantly, HomeView can act as a home hub itself. You don’t need to buy a separate HomePod or Apple TV simply to use HomeView as your smart-home hub. However, some advanced features depend on compatible accessories, an iCloud+ subscription, or an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad.
